analysis.one_liner: Raises the royalty coal companies pay on federal-land coal to 50% and bans exporting it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Energy Committee after being referred in December 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal companies mine about 40% of U.S. coal from land owned by the federal government, paying royalties set decades ago. This bill would have required them to pay at least 50 cents of every dollar of coal's value back to the public, instead of the much lower current rate. It also would have banned exporting that publicly owned coal abroad, and paused all new federal coal leases until the new rules were in place.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers, who would collect far more money for coal taken from publicly owned land, and communities affected by coal mining and coal exporting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near coal operations

how_it_helps.text: Requires coal lease royalties on federal land to be at least 50% of the coal's value for any new or renewed lease, replacing a much lower statutory minimum [S2][S3].
Directs the President to issue a rule prohibiting export of coal produced on federal land, keeping that publicly owned resource for domestic use [S2][S3].
Halts new federal coal lease sales until Interior certifies the new royalty and export rules are implemented, pausing further below-market sales in the meantime [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that mine federal land, which would pay sharply higher royalties and lose the ability to sell that coal overseas, plus port and rail businesses in the export chain.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal coal miners and coal exporters

drawbacks.text: A 50% royalty is roughly four times the current federal rate, which would raise mining costs for companies operating on federal land and could lead to layoffs in coal-dependent towns or higher prices for utilities that burn that coal, costs that can pass to electricity customers [S3].
The export ban would eliminate revenue for coal producers and for port, rail, and shipping businesses that handle export coal, and could reduce overall demand for federal coal [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public currently sells coal from its own land at royalty rates set decades ago, so the 50% rate would transfer significant money from mining companies to taxpayers. The trade-off is real: higher mining costs and a lost export market would squeeze coal companies and the communities that depend on them, and could nudge up prices for electricity from federal coal. Whether the public gain outweighs those costs depends on how much coal demand shifts versus how much more the government collects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on December 1, 2015, joined by Sens. Blumenthal and Whitehouse [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
No further action was recorded: the committee held no markup, the Senate never voted, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies mining federal land are better off, because they continue paying the old, lower royalty rate and can still export federal coal. Taxpayers did not receive the higher payments the bill would have collected.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after referral, letting it expire.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Coal mining companies on federal land
industries.note: The bill would roughly quadruple the royalty these companies pay to mine publicly owned coal and block them from exporting it, while also pausing new leases. Their gain from the bill's failure was continuing to pay the decades-old lower rate on coal taken from public land.

industries.industry: Coal export terminals, railroads, and shipping
industries.note: The export ban would have cut off federal coal as a source of export business. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against taxpayers who would own the coal. The bill's failure preserved this export chain.
Higher royalties would raise the cost of federal coal, but the export ban would keep more coal in the domestic market. The net effect on power prices is unclear.
